messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 56-year-old European American combat pilot, has been struggling with symptoms following a life-threatening accident that occurred several months ago. During his routine flight training exercise, an explosion in mid-air caused severe turbulence and left him feeling dizzy and lightheaded. This traumatic event marked the beginning of his relentless battle with PTSD. John’s dizziness and nausea became immediate triggers for intense anxiety, leading to a series of maladaptive strategies as he tried to regain control over his life. For example, after feeling ill one morning following a particularly vivid flashback, John decided to avoid hospitals and any medical examinations altogether. He was certain that these environments would only exacerbate his feelings of vulnerability. This avoidance behavior has extended into other areas; he no longer enjoys the activities he once loved, such as hiking and spending time with friends. The explosion sounds from fireworks on Independence Day have also triggered intense reactions. On one occasion, while driving home after a celebration, John felt dizzy and had to pull over. The unexpected movement nearby caused him to react as if he were in imminent danger. His heightened state of hypervigilance has become an almost constant presence; he finds himself constantly tense and on guard, anticipating the next potential explosion or dizziness spell. John's emotional numbness is palpable; he feels dead inside, a stark contrast to his once vibrant life. The accident shattered his beliefs about the world being safe and predictable. He now views the world as an inherently dangerous place, which has reinforced his sense of vulnerability and hypervigilance. Consequently, his maladaptive strategies have intensified. His strict control over eating is one way he tries to maintain a semblance of order in his life. The cycle of triggers, negative appraisals, threat perception, and maladaptive behaviors continues to tighten. John’s emotional numbness has led him to give up activities he once found pleasurable because they no longer bring the same sense of enjoyment or relief from anxiety. He is also convinced that hospitals and medical examinations will only heighten his feelings of vulnerability, thus reinforcing his avoidance behavior. His wife notices a significant change in John's demeanor; he seems withdrawn and on edge all the time. This has strained their relationship as well as his work life. His colleagues at the base have observed a marked decline in his ability to handle high-stress situations, leading to concerns about his fitness for duty. John’s maladaptive strategies have further entrenched his negative beliefs. He avoids social gatherings and medical appointments, reinforcing his emotional numbness and heightened sense of danger. The avoidance behaviors have also intensified his triggers; any sound or physical sensation that even remotely resembles the explosion now sends him into a spiral of anxiety and hypervigilance. John finally sought help after realizing that he could no longer function normally at work or in his personal life. His deepest fear is becoming entirely detached from reality, unable to engage with the world around him. He hopes for relief from his constant state of alertness and a return to feeling emotionally connected to his family and hobbies. The cycle of triggers leading to maladaptive strategies and negative appraisals has left John feeling isolated and overwhelmed. His journey towards recovery involves breaking this vicious loop, starting with understanding and addressing the specific triggers that have become so potent in his life.
